newsitem.title: BELGIUM: ANALYSTS CAUTIOUS ON RECTICEL, WARY OF SHARE.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS CAUTIOUS ON RECTICEL, WARY OF SHARE.

text.p: Earnings at Belgian Recticel SA will have improved in 1996, analysts say, but in view of the polyurethane foam products group's cyclical nature the share is only for speculative players.
Analysts foresee slightly better margins, lower financing charges and no repeat of the extraordinary charge seen in 1995.
The earnings report due out on Wednesday after the 1600 GMT bourse close is expected to show a loss per share of five francs with forecasts ranging from a profit of 19 to a loss of 10.
But all predictions are for a recovery from a 1995 loss of 24.90 francs per share.
For 1997 a further climb to a profit of 14 francs is seen.
But Recticel is unlikely to pay dividends any time soon, analysts say. They note that the company still owes a large sum in payouts to holders of cumulative preference shares.

"The backlog at the moment is 152 francs gross per cum pref share. Even if 1997 EPS were 14 francs, Recticel would still only be able to pay back 35 francs to cum pref holders," one analyst, who asked to remain anonymous, said.
He said his calculations were based on the total 27.4 million shares outstanding regardless of the class of share.
He said Recticel would continue to suffer from high financing charges because "shareholders' equity cannot grow because future profits will have to be paid to preference shareholders."
Analyst Danny Wittenberg at brokers Dewaay forecast 1996 net loss of 213.6 million francs, or 7.80 francs per share, down from 1995's 680 million franc loss, or 24.90 francs per share.

Analysts expected margins to have improved slightly as Recticel passed some of the higher raw materials costs on to customers. There would have been no exceptional costs in 1996 as the company took charges for a restructuring in full in 1995.

Some of the effects of the restructuring, involving a delocalisation in the comfort sector to low-cost eastern European countries, should have come through in 1996 with a fuller impact in 1997, analysts said.

Demand for Recticel's products would have been affected by the poor shape of the car sector, suffering from weak demand, tough competition and a need for cost controls, and a depressed European construction sector, they said.
One analyst noted that 1996 results would benefit from the absence of the heavy investments Recticel had to carry out in 1995 to meet strong BMW demand for its products.

Analyst Georges Piron at bank BBL said that costs would have remained relatively high in the first few months of 1997, but "we hope that with a better economy in Europe Recticel will begin to be able to raise prices."

In terms of price to book and book value per share Recticel stock is cheap. Technically, the ordinary share is approaching a key chart point at 347 francs, which marks the cross of trendlines linking recent lows and recent highs.
But given the highly volatile nature of Recticel's markets and the company's volatile earnings history analysts said they could not recommend holding the shares.

"I would stay away from the share...it has lagged the bourse index by a lot...but everything depends on whether there is confirmation of the turnaround, then it could be worth buying at the current level," the anonymous analyst said.
"The company is not master of its own fate...it has no grip on raw materials prices, where it has to deal with giants such as BASF ," he said.
The preference shares added three francs to close at 398 on Monday, the ordinary shares were up two at 340.

Joining in a general bourse rally, the ordinary shares are up 14 percent since the start of the year, while the preference shares have gained 12 percent. But the Bel-20 bourse index has jumped by 17 percent since the beginning of 1997.
BBL's Piron said, "If you have them (Recticels) and agree it is a speculative share, it is rather good, but I remain rather prudent."
